agent_notes: The Hebrew verse 1 carries the superscription (KJV 66:0) together with the first call to praise (KJV 66:1). I translated both as one verse. 'lamnatzeach' is glossed 'to the choirmaster' as in STEPBible; the sense 'to the director/for the leader' is traditional and its exact liturgical function is uncertain.

agent_notes: metzudah can mean 'net/snare' or 'stronghold/prison'. I chose 'net' (STEPBible, KJV, YLT, ASV) and give the 'stronghold' reading (Rashi, Metzudat Zion) in the commentary. BBE's 'prison... chains on our legs' is a paraphrase; the Hebrew says 'loins/hips', not legs.

revayah is rare (it also occurs in Ps 23:5, 'my cup overflows'), from the root ravah, 'to be saturated'. I glossed 'saturation' / 'overflowing abundance'; KJV 'wealthy place' is an old tradition, Ibn Ezra reads 'to air/open space' (la-avir), which I did not follow. Rashi's Pesikta Rabbati citation ('kings of every nation') is quoted as Rashi gives it; I did not check the Pesikta myself.

The psalm turns from the plural 'we' (vv. 1-12) to a singular 'I'. Rashi, Radak and Meiri read the singular as the voice of the whole people speaking as one; I keep the plain singular and say so in the commentary rather than choosing for the reader.

agent_notes: qeṭoret is the rising smoke of the sacrifice; KJV and ASV 'incense' is misleading because no spice is named and the burning is of rams' fat (Radak, Metzudat David). BBE 'smoke of sheep' is closer. I kept 'smoke' in both layers.

Revised per the reviewer request. The commentators split on romam: Radak and Rashi's first gloss read a verb ('I exalted him with my tongue', 'he was exalted'), Rashi's second gloss and the STEPBible tagging (H7318 noun) read a noun, 'his exaltation under my tongue'. The literal layer keeps the noun, as the tagging has it; the commentary presents the KJV verb as one defensible reading. BBE 'lifted up from the underworld' has no support in the Hebrew.

agent_notes: 'Seeing' (ra'iti) iniquity in the heart is ambiguous: 'regard, cherish' (KJV, Radak on holding evil intent) versus 'discern, find' (Rashi/Malbim read it as a confession of doubt). I translate with the neutral 'seen' in the literal layer and 'cherished' in the dramatic one, and flag the choice. BBE 'I said in my heart' misrenders the verb.

agent_notes: yekhachashu: STEPBible 'they cringe'. The root kachash is 'to lie, deceive, feign'; KJV 'submit themselves' and BBE 'forced to put themselves under your feet' are interpretive. I kept the literal 'lie/feign' in the literal layer and 'cringe' in the glosses and dramatic layer. YLT 'feign obedience' is the closest of the five.
